This petition under Section 166 MV act is filed by the Petitioner seeking compensation of Rs.1,00,00,000/- for the injuries sustained by her in a road traffic accident.

2. It is the specific case of the petitioner that on 24.05.2022 at about 9:00 to 9:15 a.m., she was proceeding on her Honda Activa scooter bearing registration No. KA-04-JA-4149 from M.S. Palya towards Gangamana Circle, near East KV School, Air Force Station, Jalahalli, Bengaluru.

entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: At that time, the driver of the tractor bearing registration No. KA-15-TA- 0144 (hereinafter referred to as the offending vehicle) drove the same at a high speed, in a rash and negligent manner, and dashed against the petitioner's vehicle from behind, thereby causing the accident.
3. As a result of the impact, the petitioner sustained serious injuries.

She was immediately shifted to the Air Force Hospital, where she was given first aid treatment, and thereafter to M.S. Ramaiah Hospital, Bengaluru, where she underwent inpatient treatment and surgery.

The petitioner asserts that, due to the injuries sustained in the accident, she is now suffering from permanent disability,
resulting in loss of earning capacity and future income, and is unable to lead a normal life as she did prior to the accident.
4. The petitioner further claims to have incurred expenses to the tune of Rs. 10,00,000/- towards medicines, treatment, conveyance, better nourishment, hospital charges, and attendant charges.
At the time of the accident, the petitioner was aged 28 years, employed as a school teacher, and earning a monthly salary of Rs. 40,000/-.
She contends that, due to the accidental injuries, she has lost her earning capacity and income.
5. The accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of the offending vehicle.
Therefore, the petitioner prays that suitable compensation be awarded against Respondent No. 1 and Respondent No. 2, being respectively the owner and insurer of the offending vehicle.
6. In response to the petition notice, Respondent No.2 appeared through counsel and filed its written statement.
Respondent No.1 appeared but not filed his written statement.

has admitted the issuance of an insurance policy in respect of the alleged offending vehicle;
however, it is specifically contended that their liability, if any, is strictly subject to the terms and conditions of the said policy.
The respondent has categorically denied the allegation of rash and negligent driving on the part of the driver of the offending vehicle.

It is further contended that, at the time of the accident, the driver of the said vehicle did not possess a valid and effective driving licence, and the vehicle itself did not have a valid permit or fitness certificate, thereby constituting violations of statutory requirements.

8. The respondent has further denied the very involvement of the offending vehicle in the alleged accident, asserting that it has been falsely implicated in collusion with the petitioner and the concerned police.

It is also the contention of the respondent that the owner of the offending vehicle and the investigating police have failed to comply with the mandatory provisions under Section 134(c) and Section 158(6) of the Motor Vehicles Act.

The respondent has further denied the nature of the injuries as alleged by the petitioner, as well as her occupation, income, disability, and the quantum of expenses claimed.
It is contended that the amount of compensation sought is highly excessive, exaggerated, and untenable.

On these grounds,
Respondent No. 2 has prayed for dismissal of the petition against it.

10. On the basis of the above pleadings, the following Issues were framed :-
1.

Whether the Petitioner proves that she sustained injuries, when she was proceeding in the Honda Activa Scooter bearing No.KA-04-JA-4149 on 24-05-2022 about 9-00 a.m. to 9.15 a.m., near K.V.School, East Air Force Road, Jalahalli,
Bengaluru District, due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of Tractor bearing No.KA-15-TA-0114?
2. What compensation petitioner is entitled ?
3. What order ?

11. In order to prove the claim, the Petitioner examined herself as PW.1 and in support of her case, 4 witnesses were examined as PW-2 to 5 and got marked the documents as per Ex.P.1 to P.28.
12.
On the other hand, the Respondent No.2 has examined FDA, RTO, Yelahanka as RW.1 and got marked documents at Ex.R.1 and Ex.R.2.
Dr.Sudhakar is examined as RW-2 and got marked the copy of MLC at Ex.R.3.

Further, official of respondent No.2 is examined as RW-3 and got marked the documents at Ex.R.4 to 7.
13.

By considering the available materials on record and the arguments addressed by the parties, I have answered the above Issues as under:
Issue No.1: In the Affirmative.
Issue No.2: Partly in affirmative.

Issue No.3: As per the final order, for the following:
REASONS 14. ISSUE NO.1:-

PW1 deposed that on 24.05.2022 at about 9:00 to 9:15 a.m., she was proceeding on her Honda Activa scooter bearing registration No. KA-04-JA-4149 from M.S. Palya towards Gangamana Circle, near East KV School, Air Force Station, Jalahalli, Bengaluru.

At that time, the driver of the offending vehicle drove the same at a high speed, in a rash and negligent manner, and dashed against the petitioner's vehicle from behind, thereby causing the accident.
As a result of the impact, the petitioner sustained serious injuries.

She was immediately shifted to the Air Force Hospital, where she was given first aid treatment, and thereafter to M.S. Ramaiah Hospital,
Bengaluru, where she underwent inpatient treatment and surgery.

15. In order to substantiate her case, the petitioner has produced police documents at Ex.P.1 to 9 namely FIR, complaint, spot mahazar, spot sketch, notice, reply, IMV report, wound certificate and Varsha.N vs Shekarappa.J.V on 3 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/179693235/
3 charge sheet.
16.

The contention of Respondent No.2 is that the offending vehicle was not at all involved in the accident, and that the petitioner, in active collusion with the police, created false documents in order to implicate the vehicle and claim compensation.

Reliance was placed on ILR 2021 KAR 146, The divisional Manager, United India Insurance Co ltd, Belagavi V Smt Reshama and others wherein the Karnataka high court has held that fraudulent claims, false complaints, and abuse of process of law cannot be permitted, and once fraud is proved, any judgment obtained cannot stand.

since the history of injury is often given orally by attendants at the time of admission.

sentences.text: 18. Coming to the evidence, PW-1 was cross- examined at length.
She specifically denied the suggestions that an auto rickshaw caused the accident or that the tractor was falsely implicated.
She denied the suggestion that the auto rickshaw had no insurance and, therefore, the tractor was wrongly implicated in collusion with police.
Her testimony remained consistent with the version in the complaint and charge sheet.
19. Respondent No.2 examined RW-2, Dr.Sudhakar, and produced Ex.R-3 MLC extract, which records history of accident as fall due to auto rickshaw.

The petitioner has pointed out that the hospital documents (Ex.P-10 and Ex.R-3), both from M.S. Ramaiah Hospital, themselves show inconsistent histories, one mentioning skid and fall, and the other involvement of auto rickshaw.
Official of the Respondent no 1 was examined as RW3 and he reiterated the contention of the written statement.
Varsha.N vs Shekarappa.

J.V on 3 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/179693235/
4 20.

As rightly pointed out by the petitioner, the hospital documents at Ex P-10 and Ex R-3, both emanating from M.S. Ramaiah Hospital, themselves disclose inconsistent histories, one attributing the cause to a skid and fall, while another records involvement of an autorickshaw.
This inherent contradiction weakens the defence of Respondent No.2 rather than strengthening it.

Importantly,
the contemporaneous complaint lodged on the very same day at 7:30 p.m. clearly mentions the offending tractor along with its registration number, and after due investigation, the police filed a charge sheet against the driver of the said vehicle.

On careful consideration of the pleadings, oral evidence, and documentary materials placed on record, it is evident that PW-1 has consistently deposed that the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending tractor and trolley.
In her cross-examination, nothing material has been elicited to discredit her testimony.
She specifically denied the suggestions that the accident occurred due to a skid and fall from a two-wheeler, or that the offending vehicle was falsely implicated in collusion with the police.

On the contrary, her evidence stands corroborated by contemporaneous police documents produced at Exs P-1 to P-9, which include the FIR, complaint, spot mahazar, spot sketch, notice, reply, IMV report,
wound certificate, and charge sheet.

21. The wound certificate and discharge summary further reflect that the petitioner sustained grievous injuries, including blunt injury to the abdomen with grade-IV laceration of the spleen and grade-III liver laceration, multiple rib fractures, bilateral pneumothorax, and vertebral fractures.

Although Ex. P-10 and R-3 refer to a history of skid and fall, and the auto rickshaw caused the accident, the inconsistency has been adequately explained and does not displace the weight of the contemporaneous complaint and subsequent investigation.
Respondent No.2 has not produced any credible evidence to rebut the charge sheet or substantiate the plea of false implication.
Reliance placed by the Respondents on decisions involving allegations of collusion or false implication is misplaced, as the facts and circumstances of those cases are clearly distinguishable.
In the present matter, no independent witness has been examined nor cogent material produced to support the plea of collusion.
If indeed collusion existed, Respondent No. 1 ought to have initiated appropriate proceedings before the Investigating Authorities or Court, which has not been done.
Mere allegations unsupported by proof cannot be accepted.
22. As held by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in MFA No. 8490/2010 presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act applies to police records unless duly rebutted.

Likewise, in 2009 (13)
SCC 530, the Hon'ble Supreme Court reiterated that in motor accident claims, the standard of proof is not beyond reasonable doubt, but on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.

Applying these principles, the case of the petitioner stands fortified by both oral and documentary evidence,
while the Respondent's defence remains unproved.
Therefore, the decisions cited by the Respondents are not applicable to the present case, and there is no false implication of the offending vehicle.
23. From the above discussion, I hold that the accident occurred solely due to rash and negligent driving by the driver of the offending vehicle, resulting in grievous injuries to the petitioner.
Issue No.1 is answered in the Affirmative.

ISSUE No.2:-

As per wound certificate and discharge summary, petitioner has sustained blunt injury to abdomen with Grade 4 laceration of the spleen and grade 3 laceration of the liver with hypovolemic shock; blunt injury to chest with bilateral rib fractures and bilateral hemopneumothorax, fracture of the right lateral epicondyle, fracture of right TP of T5 to T7 vertebrae, fracture of Left TP of L2 & L3 vertebrae, fracture of the spinous process of L4 vertebra.
25. She was immediately taken to Air Force Hospital, Bengaluru, after first aid, she was shifted to M.S.Ramaiah hospital, Bengaluru.
Where she was admitted as an inpatient and underwent surgery.

Due to the injuries sustained in the accident, the petitioner is suffering from permanent disability,
which has severally impacted her ability to lead a normal life as she did prior to the accident.

26. The Petitioner has examined MRD at M.S.Ramaiah hospital, as PW-3 and he has produced the 5 documents at Ex.P.20 to 24.
27.
The Petitioner has examined Dr.Nagaraj.B.N, an Orthopedic Surgeon at Sai Ortho and Dental Center and resident of Bangalore, as PW-4 and he has produced the 2 documents at Ex.P.25 and 26.

Further, Medical Officer at Air Force hospital, is examined as PW-5 and he has produced one document at Ex.P.28.
28. PW-4, deposed that the petitioner had sustained grievous injuries in the accident, including blunt injury to the abdomen with Grade 4 laceration of the spleen, Grade 3 liver laceration with hypovolemic shock, blunt injury to the chest with bilateral rib fractures, bilateral pneumothorax,
right lateral epicondylar fracture, fracture of right transverse process of T5 to T7 vertebra, fracture of left transverse process of L2 and L3 vertebra, and fracture of spinous process of L4 vertebra.

The petitioner underwent emergency exploratory laparotomy with splenectomy, liver mobilization,
bilateral ICD insertion, and stabilization of fractures. The epicondylar fracture was treated conservatively. PW-4
clinically and radiologically examined the petitioner to evaluate permanent disability.

He noted that the petitioner continued to suffer from pain and stiffness in the right elbow,
inability to extend the right elbow completely, difficulty in lifting weights with the left elbow, flexion deformity in the right elbow, restricted elbow movements, and tenderness with limitation in wrist extension.
PW-4 assessed permanent physical disability of the right arm at 37% and the whole-body physical disability at 12%.
However, in cross- examination, PW-4 candidly admitted that he had not treated the petitioner and had not sought opinion from the treating doctors while assessing disability.
He further admitted that external injuries had healed, there was no nerve injury, no fractures related to the elbow, and that the petitioner was treated conservatively.
He also conceded that no further surgery was required, and the disability assessed was only physical, not functional.
He also agreed that continuous use of the affected limb could gradually improve movement and reduce complaints, and the present restriction was not severe.

29. It is pertinent to note that PW-4 has not given any specific opinion regarding the functional disability, i.e., the actual impact of the physical disability on the petitioner's earning capacity and day-to-day activities.

However, considering the nature and location of injuries, particularly restriction in the right elbow which play a vital role in performing routine as well as occupational tasks, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner's professional efficiency is likely to be Varsha.N vs Shekarappa.J.V on 3 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/179693235/
6 affected.
As a teacher, frequent use of her upper limbs is required for writing on the board, handling books, and other activities.
Any impairment in the right elbow thus directly impacts both her daily life and her professional duties.

In the absence of a specific medical opinion on functional disability,
but having regard to the oral and documentary evidence and after careful appreciation of the material on record, this Tribunal fairly assesses the functional disability of the petitioner at 8% of the whole body for the limited purpose of computing future loss of earning capacity and compensation.

30. Due to the injuries sustained in the accident, the petitioner contended that she is no longer able to discharge her duties as she was performing prior to the accident, and thereby she has suffered substantial loss of income.

She stated that she was employed as a teacher in Vani High School,
Rajajinagar, Bengaluru, drawing a salary of about 40,000/- per month.

To substantiate her claim,
she has produced the relieving letter and bank statement marked at Ex P-14 and 15.

Ex P-14 discloses that the petitioner was in service with the said institution from 19-06-2017 to 23-05- 2022,
and after the accident, she was relieved from service.
Exhibit P-15 bank statement shows credit entries towards her salary, though the amount credited is not uniform and varies from month to month.
31. In further support, the petitioner examined the HR Executive of Sri Vani Education Center Trust, Rajajinagar, Bengaluru, as PW-2.
He has produced the pay slips and attendance register at Ex P-17 and P-18.
On perusal of Ex P-14, 17 and EX P-18, it is clear that the petitioner was indeed employed in the said institution.
However, the pay slips at Ex P-17 show that her salary varied from month to month.

For instance, in January 2022, she received 54,520/- (including incentives); in February 2022, 24,250/-; in March 2022, 19,588/-; in April 2022, 23,443/-; and in May 2022,
17,994/-.
Thus, it is evident that her income was fluctuating and not fixed.

32. Nevertheless, the materials on record demonstrate that the petitioner was gainfully employed in a educational institution and had good prospects in her teaching career with scope for stable and higher earnings in the future.

Considering her qualifications, experience, and the fact that she was already drawing salary in the range of 20,000/- to 23,000/-, it would be just and reasonable to take her monthly income at 20,000/- for the purpose of assessing future loss of income.
Such a determination, though lower than the highest salary drawn, balances the fluctuating nature of her income and at the same time ensures fairness to both parties.
33. In the petition the age of the petitioner is mentioned as 29 years.
Ex.P.11 Aadhar card shows that she was born on 11-10-1993.

The same is considered as age of the petitioner, then as on the date of accident he was aged 29 years and the multiplier applicable to the case on hand is 17.
34.

Thus this tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner who sustained the injuries is entitled for compensation under the following heads:
35. Loss of future income on account of permanent disability: Considering the petitioner's grievous injury which has resulted in performing daily vocational activities, this court is of the opinion that the functional disability of 8% is reasonable and just.

7 36.
The petitioner was 29 years old as on date of alleged accident and the multiplier applicable to the petitioner as per decision laid down by Hon'ble Apex court in Sarla Verma's case is at 17.
The income taken as Rs.20,000 x 12 x 17 x 8/100= Rs.3,26,400/- towards loss of future income.
37. Pain and sufferings:

So far as the compensation under non-pecuniary damages are concerned,
considering the nature of the grievous injury, which has resulted in performing daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of inpatient treatment and physical and mental suffering endured by the petitioner, this tribunal is of the opinion that an amount of .50,000/- would be just and fair compensation under head of Pain and sufferings.
38. Loss of amenities of life: undoubtedly the petitioner is suffering from difficulties in performing day to day activities and is facing continuous hardship due to the disability.
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .30,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
39. Medical expenses:
Under the pecuniary damages, expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization and medicines, the Petitioner has produced medical bills at Ex.P.12 amounting to .7,84,878/-.
There is no evidence forthcoming to disbelieve the said medical bills.
On perusal of medical bills, it appears that the petitioner has spent Rs.7,84,878/- towards medical treatment.
The medical bills appears to be genuine.
Therefore, the Petitioner is awarded compensation of .7,84,878/- towards Medical Expenses.

40. Conveyance, food, nourishment and attendant charges: Ex.P.10 - Discharge summary shows that Petitioner was treated as an inpatient at M.S.Ramaiah Hospital, Bengaluru, from 24-05-2022 to 09-06-2022, for a period of 17 days.
Therefore, it is just and reasonable to award compensation of .20,000/- under the head of conveyance, food, nourishment and attendant charges.
41. Loss of earning during laid up period:

With regard to the loss of earnings during treatment period, Considering the nature of the grievous injury, which has resulted in significant difficulty in carrying out daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of impatient treatment and recovery,
this tribunal considers the 2 months for rest is considered .

As the monthly net income of the Petitioner is already considered as 20,000/- per month, loss of earning during laid up period would be .20,000/- x 2 = Rs.40,000/- Under head loss of earning during laid up period.

42. Thus the compensation awarded under the various heads are as under:

Liability:

Respondent No.2 has contended that the owner of the offending vehicle violated the terms and conditions of the insurance policy as the driver did not possess a valid and effective licence to drive the offending vehicle at the time of the accident.

It is specifically alleged that the driver was not authorized to drive a tractor with an attached trailer,
and on this ground, Respondent No.2 has sought to avoid liability to indemnify the insured.
44. To substantiate this plea, Respondent No.2 examined the RTO, Yellanka-Bengaluru, as RW-1 and produced the driving licence extract of the driver at Ex.R-2.
As per Ex R-2, the driver was authorized to drive a tractor but not a tractor attached with a trailer.
RW-1 stated that the driver was not authorized to drive the particular class of vehicle involved in the accident.

45. Learned counsel for Respondent No.2 vehemently argued that possession of a licence for one class of vehicle does not entitle a person to drive another class, unless specifically endorsed by the licensing authority.

46. On careful consideration of the pleadings, evidence, and arguments, it is seen that Respondent No.2 has not produced any document to establish that the gross vehicle weight of the tractor and trolley exceeded the permissible limit of 7,500 kg so as to bring it within the category of transport/commercial vehicle requiring a separate endorsement.
In fact, RW-3, though an official witness, he has not stated regarding the gross weight of the offending tractor and trailer in his chief affidavit.

47. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in recent decision, Mukund Dewagan V Oriental Insurance Company Limited (2017) 14 SCC 663 has clarified that a person holding a valid licence to drive a "Light Motor Vehicle (LMV)" is competent to drive a vehicle whose gross vehicle weight does not exceed 7,500 kg,

entities.text: Mukund Dewagan V Oriental Insurance Company Limited (2017) 14 SCC 663
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, this Tribunal is unable to accept the plea of policy violation raised by Respondent No.2.
48.
Accordingly, the defence of breach of policy condition is rejected.
The Respondent No.1 being the insured, and Respondent No.2 being the insurer of the offending tractor and trailer, are held jointly and severally liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.

However, as per settled principles,
the primary liability to deposit compensation shall be on Respondent No.2- the insurer.
49. Respondent No.2 is directed to pay the awarded compensation to the petitioner with interest at 6% per annum from the date of petition till realisation.
With these observation I answer Issue No.2 partly in the affirmative.

50. ISSUE NO.3 : In view of the above discussion, reasons stated and findings given to Issues, I proceed to pass the following:

Respondent No.2 shall pay the aforesaid amount within two months from the date of this order.

After deposit of compensation amount 25% of the amount shall be kept in FD in the name of petitioner in any Nationalized or Scheduled Bank of her choice for a period of 2 years and balance 75% shall be disbursed to the petitioner through E-payment on proper identification.

Draw award accordingly.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
The contention of Respondent No.2 is that the offending vehicle was not at all involved in the accident, and that the petitioner, in active collusion with the police, created false documents in order to implicate the vehicle and claim compensation.
Reliance was placed on ILR 2021 KAR 146, The divisional Manager, United India Insurance Co ltd, Belagavi V Smt Reshama and others wherein the Karnataka high court has held that fraudulent claims, false complaints, and abuse of process of law cannot be permitted, and once fraud is proved, any judgment obtained cannot stand.
Applying these principles, the case of the petitioner stands fortified by both oral and documentary evidence,
while the Respondent's defence remains unproved.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Reliance was also placed on 2009 (13) SCC 530 BIMLA DEVI AND OTHERS V HIMACHAL ROAD TRANSPORT CORPORATION AND OTHERS where the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that strict proof beyond reasonable doubt is not required in claim proceedings, and proof on the basis of preponderance of probabilities is sufficient.
Respondent No.2 has not produced any credible evidence to rebut the charge sheet or substantiate the plea of false implication.
Reliance placed by the Respondents on decisions involving allegations of collusion or false implication is misplaced, as the facts and circumstances of those cases are clearly distinguishable.
In the present matter, no independent witness has been examined nor cogent material produced to support the plea of collusion.
If indeed collusion existed, Respondent No. 1 ought to have initiated appropriate proceedings before the Investigating Authorities or Court, which has not been done.
Mere allegations unsupported by proof cannot be accepted.
22. As held by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in MFA No. 8490/2010 presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act applies to police records unless duly rebutted.
Therefore, the decisions cited by the Respondents are not applicable to the present case, and there is no false implication of the offending vehicle.
Any impairment in the right elbow thus directly impacts both her daily life and her professional duties.
Considering her qualifications, experience, and the fact that she was already drawing salary in the range of 20,000/- to 23,000/-, it would be just and reasonable to take her monthly income at 20,000/- for the purpose of assessing future loss of income.
Such a determination, though lower than the highest salary drawn, balances the fluctuating nature of her income and at the same time ensures fairness to both parties.

opennyai_summary.decision:
Accordingly, the defence of breach of policy condition is rejected.
The Respondent No.1 being the insured, and Respondent No.2 being the insurer of the offending tractor and trailer, are held jointly and severally liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.
However, as per settled principles,
the primary liability to deposit compensation shall be on Respondent No.2- the insurer.
49. Respondent No.2 is directed to pay the awarded compensation to the petitioner with interest at 6% per annum from the date of petition till realisation.
With these observation I answer Issue No.2 partly in the affirmative.

9 ORDER Claim Petition filed under Sec.166 of M.V.Act is allowed in part with cost.
Petitioner is awarded compensation of Rs.12,51,278/- together with interest @ 6%
p.a. from the date of petition till the date of deposit with the Tribunal.
Respondent No.2 shall pay the aforesaid amount within two months from the date of this order.
After deposit of compensation amount 25% of the amount shall be kept in FD in the name of petitioner in any Nationalized or Scheduled Bank of her choice for a period of 2 years and balance 75% shall be disbursed to the petitioner through E-payment on proper identification.
Advocate's fee is fixed at .1,000/-.
Draw award accordingly.
